explanations.explanation: Paul, the apostle, asks that question, but he doesn't say yes to it. His very next words are "Certainly not!" (Romans 6:2). That's like dumping a whole bowl of dough on the floor so the cleanup crew gets more practice. Nobody says, "Great idea, do it again."

Paul asks the question out loud, then shuts it down right away: "Certainly not!" He follows with, "How can we who died to sin live in it any longer?" So what he's really saying is that sinning more to get more grace makes no sense for people who died to sin. Good ear, friend.

That's his reason, right there in verse 2: "How can we who died to sin live in it any longer?" Paul doesn't say believers are trying hard to hold back. He says they died to sin. A person who has died isn't going back to the old house.

I get why a promise sounds right, because people make them all the time. Paul never mentions one here, though. His reason is that believers "died to sin" (Romans 6:2). That's something that happened to them, not something they swore.

Law is a word Paul does use in this passage, but not here. In verse 2 his reason is that believers "died to sin." Law shows up later, when he says they are "not under law, but under grace" (Romans 6:14). So this answer is close to the neighborhood but at the wrong house.

That's the one: "…we too may walk in newness of life." Christ was raised through the glory of the Father, and Paul says believers may walk in newness of life too. Notice he says walk. That's an everyday, one-foot-in-front-of-the-other kind of word, not a once-a-year kind.

Rest sounds lovely, friend, and I'm a stamper who knows a good rest. But Paul doesn't say that in verse 4. He says believers may "walk in newness of life." Walking means moving, so this life has some steps in it.
That's a big job title, and it isn't in this verse. Paul keeps it down to earth: "…we too may walk in newness of life." Nobody's handing out crowns here. They're handing out a new way to walk.

Yes, and Paul says it with confidence: "For if we have been united with Him like this in His death, we will certainly also be united with Him in His resurrection." Look at that word certainly. Paul isn't saying maybe or we'll see. He's saying it's settled.

Paul says the opposite. Verse 5 reads, "For if we have been united with Him like this in His death, we will certainly also be united with Him in His resurrection." The word certainly doesn't leave a crack in the door. Believers united with Christ in His death will be united with Him in His resurrection.

Right there in verse 6: "…that we should no longer be slaves to sin." The old self was crucified with Christ so that sin's grip would be rendered powerless. Paul is saying sin lost its hold, and it doesn't get to boss believers around anymore.

I can see why you'd pick it, since death is all over this passage. But Paul doesn't say it in verse 6. He says the old self was crucified so that "we should no longer be slaves to sin." Slavery is the word to hold onto.

That's a warm thought, but it's not what Paul says in verse 6. He says the point is that "we should no longer be slaves to sin." He does talk about being united with Christ in verse 5. Still, the thing believers are done being is a slave to sin.

Paul says the reverse, and he says it plainly. Verse 9 reads, "…since Christ was raised from the dead, He cannot die again; death no longer has dominion over Him." Cannot die again. There's no second round.

Right, and Paul puts it in two parts: "He cannot die again; death no longer has dominion over Him." Christ was raised from the dead, and death doesn't rule Him. That's the kind of fact you can lean your whole weight on.
Paul says it just like that: "The death He died, He died to sin once for all." It's finished. No repeat, no encore, and nobody needs to do it again.
That's not it, friend. Paul says, "The death He died, He died to sin once for all." Once for all is the opposite of again and again. The one time covered it.

A yearly schedule sounds organized, but Paul doesn't have one. Verse 10 says, "The death He died, He died to sin once for all." Once for all means no calendar reminders. And right after that, he says the life Christ lives, He lives to God.

Yes, and the contrast is the whole point: "instruments of wickedness" on one side, "instruments of righteousness" on the other. Paul says to present yourselves to God as those brought from death to life. Then the parts of the body go to Him too, as instruments of righteousness. Same hands, new boss.

Strength is a nice word, but it isn't what Paul writes. The verse says to present the parts of your body to God "as instruments of righteousness." He sets that against "instruments of wickedness." Righteousness is the word that matches.

Comfort sounds cozy, and I do love a warm oven. Paul's word is different, though. He says to present the parts of your body to God "as instruments of righteousness," the opposite of "instruments of wickedness." Instruments are for doing something, and the something is righteousness.

That's the reason he gives: "For sin shall not be your master, because you are not under law, but under grace." Grace is where Paul started this whole passage, when he asked about grace increasing. Now he closes on it. Believers live under grace, and sin doesn't get to be their master.
Judgment is a heavy word, and it's not Paul's word here. Verse 14 says, "…you are not under law, but under grace." Grace is what believers stand under, and that's why sin isn't their master.

Fear can feel like it runs the show sometimes, friend. But Paul doesn't say it in verse 14. He says, "…you are not under law, but under grace." Grace is where believers stand, and sin doesn't get to be their master.
